text: Your Chapter 6 ETL script runs on a schedule now, with nobody watching the terminal. If it fails at 3 a.m., print output just disappears when the process exits — there's nothing to look back at. That's exactly the gap the logging module fills.

basicConfig sets the format for the entire script, once. Percent asctime adds a timestamp, percent levelname adds the severity — INFO, WARNING, ERROR — and percent message is whatever you pass to the logger call. Call logger dot info, warning, or error, and every message comes out consistently formatted.

Logging has five levels, and they exist so you can filter noise without deleting anything. Debug is the noisiest, then info, warning, error, and critical. Set level equals logging dot INFO in basicConfig and debug calls get silently skipped — switch it to DEBUG temporarily when you're actually troubleshooting, then switch it back.

Here's logging wired into a real pipeline step. Notice the percent d placeholder with the argument passed separately, instead of an f-string — that formatting only happens if the message actually gets logged. And logger dot exception is the one to reach for inside an except block: it's error, plus the full traceback, which is exactly what you want when a transform step breaks unexpectedly.

A handler decides where a log message actually goes. Set up a FileHandler and a StreamHandler together, and every message shows up on screen while you're watching, but it's also saved to etl_run.log — that log file is what you'd check the morning after a run nobody was there to see.

Next up: pytest. You've got functions like validate_row deciding whether data is clean enough to load — now you'll learn to test them directly, in isolation, instead of running the whole pipeline just to check one function still works.
